sectionTitle: Uses and applications of electromagnetic waves

specStatements.text: Electromagnetic waves have many practical applications. For example:
• infrared – electrical heaters, cooking food, infrared cameras
• ultraviolet – energy efficient lamps, sun tanning
• X-rays and gamma rays – medical imaging and treatments.
(HT only) Students should be able to give brief explanations why each type of electromagnetic wave is suitable for the practical application.

scopeNotes.statement: Electromagnetic waves have many practical applications. For example:
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification introduces its list with 'For example', so the six bulleted pairings are exemplars rather than an exhaustive list. The content teaches exactly the applications the specification names – television and radio; satellite communications and cooking food; electrical heaters, cooking food and infrared cameras; fibre optic communications; energy efficient lamps and sun tanning; medical imaging and treatments – and nothing is assessed that depends on an application the specification does not name. Where a familiar everyday device is mentioned (a grill, a fluorescent tube, a thermal imaging camera) it is only as an instance of an application already listed, never as an extra requirement.

scopeNotes.statement: (HT only) Students should be able to give brief explanations why each type of electromagnetic wave is suitable for the practical application.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification asks for BRIEF explanations, so each explanation is built from one or two properties that the specification itself supplies elsewhere in 4.6.2 – relative wavelength and frequency, whether the wave is transmitted, absorbed or reflected, and whether it is ionising. Mechanisms beyond GCSE are not taught: total internal reflection is not named, photon energy is not used, no account is given of dielectric heating, molecular resonance, fluorescence at the atomic level, or the biology of melanin production beyond the fact that ultraviolet absorbed by skin darkens it and can damage cells. Nothing in this material asks a student to explain an application the specification does not list, and every explanation item is marked Higher tier because the statement is HT only.

concepts.term: Practical application of an electromagnetic wave
concepts.definition: A use that is made of one part of the electromagnetic spectrum. The specification pairs each group with examples: radio waves with television and radio; microwaves with satellite communications and cooking food; infrared with electrical heaters, cooking food and infrared cameras; visible light with fibre optic communications; ultraviolet with energy efficient lamps and sun tanning; X-rays and gamma rays with medical imaging and treatments.
Television and radio programmes are broadcast as radio waves. A transmitter sends the signal out as radio waves and the aerial of a television set or radio receiver picks it up.

Microwaves carry signals between the ground and satellites in orbit. A dish on the ground transmits a microwave signal up to the satellite, which sends it back down to a receiver somewhere else on the Earth. Satellite television and satellite phone links work in this way.
A microwave oven cooks food using microwaves. The microwaves are absorbed by the food and the energy they transfer raises the temperature of the food.

concepts.term: Infrared – electrical heaters and cooking food
concepts.definition: Electrical heaters such as radiant bar heaters, and cooking appliances such as grills, toasters and conventional ovens, emit infrared radiation. The infrared is absorbed by the surfaces it reaches – a person, a room, or the food – and transfers energy to them.

An infrared camera (a thermal imaging camera) detects the infrared radiation given out by objects and turns it into an image. Hotter and cooler parts of a scene show up differently, and no visible light is needed.
Fibre optic communications send information along very thin, very pure glass fibres as pulses of visible light. Telephone, television and broadband signals are carried this way.

An energy efficient lamp of the fluorescent type produces ultraviolet inside its tube. The ultraviolet is absorbed by a coating on the inside of the tube, and the coating gives out visible light, which is what lights the room.

Ultraviolet from the Sun, or from the lamps in a sunbed, is absorbed by the skin and makes it darken – a suntan. Ultraviolet is ionising, so this exposure also carries a risk of damage to skin cells and of skin cancer.

X-rays are used to form images of the inside of the body. They are transmitted through soft tissue but absorbed by denser material such as bone or metal, so a shadow image forms on the detector behind the patient. High-energy X-rays are also used in treatment, to destroy tumours.

concepts.term: Gamma rays – medical imaging and treatments
concepts.definition: Gamma rays are used in medicine in two ways: a gamma-emitting tracer given to a patient can be detected from outside the body to show how an organ is working, and a beam of gamma rays can be directed at a tumour to destroy cancer cells.

concepts.term: Why radio waves suit television and radio
concepts.definition: Radio waves have the longest wavelengths in the spectrum, so they spread around obstacles such as hills and buildings and reach receivers that are not in a direct line from the transmitter. They are not absorbed much as they travel, so a broadcast covers a large area, and they are not ionising, so broadcasting them over towns and cities is safe.

Microwaves pass through the Earth’s atmosphere, including the ionosphere, without being strongly absorbed or reflected, so a signal can travel up to a satellite and back down again. Longer-wavelength radio waves are reflected by the ionosphere and would not get through. Microwaves can also be sent as a narrow beam onto a dish, which keeps the signal strong.

The microwaves used in an oven are absorbed by water in the food, and the energy transferred raises the temperature of that water. Microwaves penetrate a few centimetres below the surface, so energy is transferred through a layer of the food rather than only to the outside, and conduction then spreads it to the rest.

concepts.term: Why infrared suits heaters and cooking food
concepts.definition: Infrared is strongly absorbed by the surfaces of objects, including skin and food, and the energy transferred raises their temperature. Because it is a wave it travels directly from the heater or grill to whatever is in front of it, warming that object without having to warm the air on the way.

Every object emits infrared radiation, and a hotter object emits more of it, so a camera that detects infrared is detecting radiation the objects give out themselves. It therefore works in complete darkness, and differences in the infrared detected show up as differences in temperature.

concepts.term: Why visible light suits fibre optic communications
concepts.definition: Visible light is hardly absorbed by very pure glass, so it travels a long way along a fibre without the signal fading. It is reflected from the walls of the fibre, so it stays inside and follows the fibre around bends instead of escaping. Its very short wavelength and high frequency allow a large amount of information to be carried.

concepts.term: Why ultraviolet suits energy efficient lamps
concepts.definition: The ultraviolet made inside the lamp is absorbed by the coating on the tube, which gives out visible light. Almost all of the energy supplied is therefore transferred as light rather than being wasted heating a filament, which is what makes the lamp efficient. The coating and glass also stop the ultraviolet leaving the lamp.

Ultraviolet has a higher frequency and a shorter wavelength than visible light and is ionising, so when it is absorbed by the skin it can change the cells there, making them produce more dark pigment. Visible light and infrared from the Sun do not cause this change; infrared only warms the skin.

X-rays are transmitted through low-density soft tissue but absorbed by denser bone and by metal, so the pattern of radiation reaching the detector is a shadow of the structures inside the body. They travel in straight lines, so the shadow is sharp, and the image is obtained without any surgery.

concepts.term: Why gamma rays suit medical imaging and treatments
concepts.definition: Gamma rays are very penetrating, so those emitted by a tracer inside a patient pass out through the body and can be detected outside it. They are also ionising and carry a great deal of energy, so a beam aimed at a tumour damages and kills the cancer cells there.

misconceptions.question: Food in a microwave oven is heated from the middle outwards, so the centre is always the hottest part.
misconceptions.correct: Microwaves are absorbed by the food and transfer energy to it; they penetrate a short distance into the food and energy then spreads through the rest of it.
misconceptions.misconception: Microwaves go straight to the middle of the food and cook it from the inside out, so the outside stays cool.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase ‘cooks from the inside out’ is repeated so often that students take it literally. It also seems to explain why microwaved food can be hot in the middle and cool at the edges – which is really uneven absorption and uneven spreading of energy.
misconceptions.correction: Microwaves are absorbed as they enter the food, mainly in the outer few centimetres, and energy then spreads inwards by conduction. A microwave oven heats a thick piece of food faster than a grill does because energy is delivered throughout that outer layer rather than only to the surface, not because it starts in the centre.

misconceptions.question: Does food cooked in a microwave oven become radioactive?
misconceptions.correct: No. Microwaves transfer energy to the food, but they do not make it radioactive.
misconceptions.misconception: Microwaves are a kind of radiation, so they make the food radioactive, which is why microwaved food is bad for you.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word ‘radiation’ is used both for electromagnetic waves and for the emissions from radioactive substances, and news stories about radioactivity attach the word to danger. ‘Microwave radiation’ then sounds like the same thing as nuclear radiation.
misconceptions.correction: Microwaves sit in the low-frequency half of the spectrum and are not ionising. They are absorbed by the food, transfer energy to it and warm it; nothing about the food is changed into a radioactive substance. Only the far end of the spectrum – ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays – is ionising, and even those do not make an object radioactive here.

misconceptions.question: How does an infrared camera produce an image of a person in a dark room?
misconceptions.correct: It detects the infrared radiation that the person and the surroundings emit.
misconceptions.misconception: The camera shines a beam of infrared out, like an invisible torch, and photographs what it lights up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every camera a student has used needs light, and the flash on a phone reinforces the idea that a camera provides its own illumination. ‘Infrared’ is then imagined as invisible torchlight.
misconceptions.correction: Objects emit infrared radiation themselves, and hotter objects emit more of it. An infrared camera is a detector: it collects the infrared coming from the scene and converts it into an image, which is why it works in complete darkness and shows how hot different parts of the scene are.

misconceptions.question: A fibre optic cable is coiled up and bent round corners inside a building. Does the signal still get through?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The light is reflected from the walls of the fibre, so it stays inside and follows the bends.
misconceptions.misconception: Light only travels in straight lines, so a bent cable must lose the signal or need mirrors at each corner.
misconceptions.whyItArises: ‘Light travels in straight lines’ is taught early and firmly, and students meet no everyday object in which light is made to follow a curved path, so a bent light path looks impossible.
misconceptions.correction: The light does travel in straight lines between reflections. Each time it meets the wall of the fibre at a shallow angle it is reflected back into the fibre, so a series of straight paths carries it round a gentle bend. Nothing is added at the corners, and because pure glass absorbs visible light so weakly the signal stays strong over long distances.

misconceptions.question: An energy efficient fluorescent lamp makes ultraviolet inside its tube. What lights the room?
misconceptions.correct: Visible light, given out by the coating on the inside of the tube after it absorbs the ultraviolet.
misconceptions.misconception: The ultraviolet itself comes out of the lamp and lights the room, so these lamps shine ultraviolet at you.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The specification pairs ultraviolet with energy efficient lamps, so students reasonably assume the ultraviolet is what leaves the lamp. Warnings about ultraviolet then make the lamp sound dangerous.
misconceptions.correction: The ultraviolet is produced inside the tube and is absorbed by the coating on the inner surface, which gives out visible light. It is that visible light which leaves the lamp and lights the room; the coating and the glass stop almost all the ultraviolet getting out.

misconceptions.question: Why does a day spent in the Sun leave a person with a suntan?
misconceptions.correct: Ultraviolet from the Sun is absorbed by the skin and makes it darken.
misconceptions.misconception: The Sun’s heat causes the tan – it is the infrared, the part you can feel warming your skin, that browns it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Tanning happens on hot days and comes with the feeling of warmth, so the sensation of heat is taken to be the cause. Ultraviolet cannot be seen or felt, so it is easy to overlook.
misconceptions.correction: It is ultraviolet, not infrared, that tans the skin. Infrared is absorbed at the surface and simply warms it. Ultraviolet has a higher frequency, is ionising, and when absorbed changes cells in the skin so they produce more dark pigment – which is also why exposure raises the risk of skin cancer. Skin can tan on a cool, bright day and can burn in the shade.

misconceptions.question: An X-ray image of a hand shows the bones as light areas. Which parts absorbed the X-rays?
misconceptions.correct: The bone absorbed the X-rays; the soft tissue transmitted them to the detector.
misconceptions.misconception: X-rays go through the hard bone and are stopped by the soft flesh, which is why the bones show up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that X-rays are penetrating and picture them punching through the hardest material of all, and they read the light bones on the image as ‘where the X-rays got through’ rather than ‘where they did not’.
misconceptions.correction: Dense material absorbs X-rays; soft tissue lets most of them pass. The detector is darkened where X-rays reach it, so the shadow behind the bone stays light. The bright region on the image is exactly where the X-rays were absorbed, which is why metal objects also appear light.

misconceptions.question: X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and can damage cells. Can they still be used on patients?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. They are used for medical imaging, and their ionising effect is used to destroy cancer cells.
misconceptions.misconception: Ionising radiation only ever harms living things, so no doctor would deliberately aim it at a patient.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Teaching about the hazards of ionising radiation is emphatic, and students carry away a single rule – ionising means harmful – without the idea that a controlled dose aimed at the right place can do more good than harm.
misconceptions.correction: The hazard is real and doses are kept as low as possible, but that is a reason for care, not a reason never to use them. Imaging uses a small dose to gain information that could not be obtained without surgery. In treatment the ionising effect is the point: a beam is aimed at the tumour so that the cancer cells receive a high dose and the surrounding tissue receives much less.

misconceptions.question: Why are radio waves, rather than other electromagnetic waves, used to broadcast television and radio?
misconceptions.correct: Their long wavelength lets them spread around obstacles, and they are not absorbed much as they travel.
misconceptions.misconception: Radio waves travel faster than the other electromagnetic waves, so they get to the receiver first and best.
misconceptions.whyItArises: ‘Long wave’, ‘fast’ and ‘strong’ get blurred into one idea of a better wave, and the fact that broadcasts arrive instantly suggests exceptional speed rather than an ordinary property of all electromagnetic waves.
misconceptions.correction: All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed through a vacuum, so speed cannot be the reason for choosing one part of the spectrum. Radio waves are chosen because their long wavelength lets them spread around hills and buildings, they are not strongly absorbed by the atmosphere, and they are not ionising, so broadcasting them over populated areas is safe.

misconceptions.question: Which type of electromagnetic wave carries signals between the ground and a communications satellite?
misconceptions.correct: Microwaves.
misconceptions.misconception: Radio waves – they travel the furthest of all the waves, so they must be the ones that reach into space.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Radio waves are firmly linked with long-distance broadcasting, and ‘furthest’ sounds like the property needed to reach a satellite. Students also hear ‘radio signal’ used loosely for any transmitted signal.
misconceptions.correction: The specification pairs satellite communications with microwaves. Long-wavelength radio waves are reflected by the ionosphere, so they do not reach a satellite at all; microwaves pass through the atmosphere and the ionosphere with little absorption, so they can travel up and back down.

misconceptions.question: Which type of electromagnetic wave cooks bread in a toaster or food under a grill?
misconceptions.correct: Infrared.
misconceptions.misconception: Microwaves – microwaves are the waves that cook food, so any appliance that cooks must be using them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The specification pairs microwaves with cooking food, and the microwave oven is the appliance students know by name, so ‘cooking’ and ‘microwaves’ become fixed together.
misconceptions.correction: The specification pairs cooking food with microwaves and with infrared, because different appliances use different parts of the spectrum. A grill, toaster or radiant heater emits infrared, which is absorbed by the surface of the food and browns it. Only a microwave oven cooks with microwaves.

misconceptions.question: What is a broadband signal made of as it travels along a fibre optic cable?
misconceptions.correct: Pulses of visible light.
misconceptions.misconception: It is a microwave or radio signal, the same as wi-fi – all modern communication is done with those waves.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Home internet is met mainly as a wireless service, and the word ‘broadband’ is attached to both the cable and the wi-fi in the house, so the two are treated as one technology.
misconceptions.correction: The specification pairs fibre optic communications with visible light. The signal travels along a thin glass fibre as pulses of light, reflected from the walls of the fibre so that it stays inside. Microwaves and radio waves travel through the air to an aerial or dish; they are not what carries the signal down the fibre.

misconceptions.question: How does a microwave signal from a dish on the ground reach a satellite in orbit?
misconceptions.correct: It passes through the atmosphere, including the ionosphere, without being strongly absorbed or reflected.
misconceptions.misconception: The atmosphere reflects the microwaves upwards, bouncing them off the sky and on to the satellite.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet the idea that the ionosphere reflects radio waves and apply it to every transmitted signal, so reflection becomes the general way that signals get anywhere.
misconceptions.correction: Reflection by the ionosphere is what long-wavelength radio waves do, and it is precisely why they cannot be used for satellite links. Microwaves are chosen because they are transmitted through the atmosphere and the ionosphere, so a beam sent up from a dish reaches the satellite and the reply reaches the ground.

misconceptions.question: An electric bar heater warms a person standing in front of it in a cold room. How?
misconceptions.correct: Infrared travels from the heater to the person and is absorbed by their skin, transferring energy to it.
misconceptions.misconception: The heater warms the air first, and it is the warm air moving across the room that then warms the person.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Convection is the mechanism students meet most often for heating a room, and the air near a heater really is warmed, so it is taken to be the only route by which energy arrives.
misconceptions.correction: Infrared radiation travels directly from the heater to whatever is in front of it and is absorbed by that surface, which is why the warmth is felt at once and stops the instant something blocks the path. The air is warmed too, but the radiation does not need the air – it would cross a vacuum just as well.

misconceptions.question: Which type of electromagnetic wave carries a television broadcast to an aerial on a roof?
misconceptions.correct: Radio waves.
misconceptions.misconception: Microwaves – radio programmes use radio waves, but television is newer, so television must use something else.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The names ‘radio wave’ and ‘radio programme’ look like a matched pair, so television seems to need a different wave, and satellite television being real makes microwaves the obvious guess.
misconceptions.correction: The specification pairs radio waves with both television and radio. A broadcast picked up by a rooftop aerial arrives as radio waves. Microwaves are used for the satellite link when television is delivered by satellite, but that is the satellite communications application, not the broadcast to the aerial.

misconceptions.question: A television is switched over using an infrared remote control. Does the programme also arrive as infrared?
misconceptions.correct: No. The programme is broadcast as radio waves; only the remote control uses infrared.
misconceptions.misconception: The television works on infrared, because that is the wave the remote control sends to it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The one invisible signal a student has seen described for a television is the remote control’s infrared, so it becomes the wave associated with televisions in general.
misconceptions.correction: Two different applications are involved. Infrared travels a few metres from the handset to the television. The programme itself is broadcast as radio waves from a transmitter, which is the application the specification lists, and it is picked up by the aerial.

misconceptions.question: Are infrared and microwaves the same kind of wave?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum, with microwaves having the longer wavelength.
misconceptions.misconception: They are two names for the same waves – the ones that heat things up when they are absorbed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are invisible, both are met almost entirely through appliances that heat food, and the spectrum diagram places them next to each other, so the distinction collapses.
misconceptions.correction: They are neighbouring groups in the spectrum but they are used differently because they behave differently. Microwaves are absorbed by water and penetrate a few centimetres into food, and they pass through the atmosphere, which is why they suit satellite links. Infrared is absorbed at the surface of an object, which is why it suits grills, heaters and thermal cameras.

misconceptions.question: How does information travel along a fibre optic cable?
misconceptions.correct: As pulses of visible light travelling along a thin glass fibre.
misconceptions.misconception: As an electric current, because a cable is a wire and cables carry electricity to things.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other cable in the house carries electricity, and the word ‘cable’ itself implies a wire, so a fibre is pictured as a very thin metal conductor.
misconceptions.correction: The fibre is glass, not metal, and it carries no current. A transmitter turns the information into pulses of visible light, the light is reflected from the walls of the fibre so it stays inside all the way along, and a detector at the far end turns the pulses back into an electrical signal.

misconceptions.question: Can ultraviolet be seen?
misconceptions.correct: No. Ultraviolet lies beyond the violet end of the visible spectrum, so the eye does not detect it.
misconceptions.misconception: Ultraviolet is the purple light you see coming out of a UV lamp at a bowling alley or a disco.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Lamps sold as ‘UV lamps’ do glow purple, and things fluoresce brightly under them, so the visible purple glow is taken to be the ultraviolet itself.
misconceptions.correction: The purple glow is visible light that the lamp also emits, and the bright colours are visible light given out by objects that absorb the ultraviolet. The ultraviolet itself is invisible. That is exactly the effect used in an energy efficient lamp, where a coating absorbs ultraviolet and gives out visible light.

misconceptions.question: How is a medical X-ray image formed?
misconceptions.correct: X-rays pass through the patient and the pattern that reaches the detector behind them forms the image.
misconceptions.misconception: It is a photograph: the X-rays bounce off the bones and come back to the camera, like light off a mirror.
misconceptions.whyItArises: ‘Taking an X-ray’ sounds like taking a photograph, and everyday images are formed by reflected light, so reflection is assumed here too.
misconceptions.correction: Nothing is reflected back to a camera. The source is on one side of the patient and the detector on the other; bone absorbs the X-rays and soft tissue transmits them, so the image is a shadow. Gamma imaging works the other way round again: the tracer inside the patient emits the gamma rays, which pass out of the body to a detector.

misconceptions.question: Radio waves get past a hill and gamma rays get through a body. Is that the same property?
misconceptions.correct: No. Spreading around a large obstacle depends on a long wavelength; passing through matter depends on high frequency and energy.
misconceptions.misconception: It is all one thing – how strong the wave is. A strong wave gets through anything, and a weak one gets stopped.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students collapse several properties into a single scale of ‘strength’ because both examples end with the signal arriving. Nothing in everyday language separates spreading around an obstacle from penetrating it.
misconceptions.correction: The two are opposite ends of the spectrum. Radio waves have the longest wavelengths and the lowest frequencies; they spread around hills and buildings but are readily blocked by matter. Gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths and the highest frequencies, carry the most energy and are ionising; they travel in straight lines and pass through matter. A wave cannot be good at both for the same reason.

mcqs.stem: Which of these correctly pairs an application with the type of electromagnetic wave used?

options.text: Fibre optic communications – visible light
options.rationale: The specification pairs fibre optic communications with visible light; the signal travels along the glass fibre as pulses of light.

options.text: Satellite communications – radio waves
options.rationale: Radio waves are linked with long-distance broadcasting, so a student assumes they also reach a satellite; in fact microwaves are used.

options.text: Cooking food in a toaster – microwaves
options.rationale: A student who ties all cooking to microwaves picks this; a toaster cooks with infrared.

options.text: Medical imaging of bone – ultraviolet
options.rationale: Ultraviolet sits next to X-rays in the spectrum and is known to be harmful, so it gets chosen for the medical use.

mcqs.stem: Which type of electromagnetic wave carries a television broadcast to a rooftop aerial?

options.text: Microwaves
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who thinks radio waves are only for radio and that television must use something else.

options.text: Infrared
options.rationale: Chosen because the remote control uses infrared, so infrared is associated with televisions.

options.text: Ultraviolet
options.rationale: Picked as another invisible wave, with no application to televisions in the specification.

options.text: Radio waves
options.rationale: The specification pairs radio waves with television and radio.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an application of microwaves?

options.text: Sending a signal up to a satellite
options.rationale: The specification pairs microwaves with satellite communications.

options.text: Toasting a slice of bread in a grill
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who links all cooking with microwaves; a grill uses infrared.

options.text: Sending broadband down a glass fibre
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who thinks all modern signals are microwaves; the fibre carries visible light.

options.text: Taking an image of a broken bone
options.rationale: Medical imaging is paired with X-rays and gamma rays, not with microwaves.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about cooking food in a microwave oven is correct?

options.text: The microwaves make the food itself slightly radioactive as it cooks.
options.rationale: Chosen because 'radiation' is read as radioactivity; microwaves are not ionising and leave nothing radioactive.

options.text: The microwaves are absorbed by the food and transfer energy to it.
options.rationale: This is the application as the specification gives it: microwaves absorbed by the food raise its temperature.

options.text: The microwaves heat the middle of the food long before the outside.
options.rationale: The familiar phrase 'cooks from the inside out' makes this sound right.

options.text: The microwaves are reflected by the food and pass back into the oven.
options.rationale: Reflection by the metal walls is real, but food that reflected the microwaves would never warm up.

mcqs.stem: A rescue team uses an infrared camera to find a person in a dark building. How does the camera form its image?

options.text: It shines a beam of infrared out and photographs what it lights up.
options.rationale: Every camera a student has used needs light, so infrared is imagined as an invisible torch.

options.text: It detects the infrared radiation emitted by the person and the room.
options.rationale: Objects emit infrared, and a hotter object emits more, so the camera needs no light source of its own.

options.text: It detects the warm air that has risen from the person's body.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who thinks infrared is warm air rather than a wave.

options.text: It collects the small amount of visible light left in the room.
options.rationale: Plausible for night-vision generally, but then the camera would fail in complete darkness.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the waves used to cook food is correct?

options.text: A grill, a toaster and a microwave oven all cook their food using microwaves.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who ties every cooking appliance to microwaves.

options.text: Infrared and microwaves are simply two different names for the same wave.
options.rationale: Both are invisible and both heat food, so the two groups get merged.

options.text: A grill cooks with infrared and a microwave oven cooks with microwaves.
options.rationale: The specification lists cooking food under both infrared and microwaves, because different appliances use different waves.

options.text: A grill cooks with microwaves and a microwave oven cooks using infrared.
options.rationale: The straight reversal, picked by a student guessing which name goes where.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about fibre optic communications is correct?

options.text: Information travels along the fibre as pulses of electric current.
options.rationale: 'Cable' suggests a wire, and every other cable in the house carries electricity.

options.text: Information is beamed through the air as microwaves, like wi-fi.
options.rationale: Home internet is met mainly as a wireless service, so the two get merged.

options.text: Information travels along the glass fibre as pulses of visible light.
options.rationale: The specification pairs fibre optic communications with visible light.

options.text: Information travels along the fibre as pulses of invisible ultraviolet.
options.rationale: Picked as an invisible wave, but the specification pairs the fibre with visible light.

mcqs.stem: An energy efficient fluorescent lamp produces ultraviolet inside its tube. What mainly leaves the lamp and lights the room?

options.text: Visible light, produced by the coating on the inside of the tube.
options.rationale: The coating absorbs the ultraviolet and emits visible light, and it is that light which lights the room.

options.text: Ultraviolet, since that is exactly what the lamp is designed to produce.
options.rationale: The pairing of ultraviolet with the lamp makes students assume the ultraviolet comes out.

options.text: Ultraviolet, which is the purple light that the human eye can see.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who thinks the purple glow of a UV lamp is the ultraviolet.

options.text: Infrared, because the lamp becomes warmer while it is switched on.
options.rationale: Lamps do warm up, but the point of this lamp is that little energy is wasted that way.

mcqs.stem: Why does a day spent outdoors in the Sun leave a person with a suntan?

options.text: Infrared from the Sun heats the skin, which turns it a darker colour.
options.rationale: The warmth is what a person feels, so heating is taken to be the cause.

options.text: Visible light is absorbed by the skin and adds colour to it.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who does not separate ultraviolet from the light that can be seen.

options.text: X-rays from the Sun pass into the skin and change its colour.
options.rationale: X-rays are known to be penetrating, but tanning is a surface effect caused by ultraviolet.

options.text: Ultraviolet from the Sun is absorbed by the skin and makes it darken.
options.rationale: The specification pairs ultraviolet with sun tanning; absorbed ultraviolet changes cells in the skin.

mcqs.stem: An X-ray image of a hand shows the bones as light areas on a dark background. Why?

options.text: Bone transmits the X-rays, while soft tissue absorbs them.
options.rationale: Students picture penetrating X-rays punching through the hardest material.

options.text: Bone absorbs the X-rays, while soft tissue transmits them.
options.rationale: Where the X-rays are absorbed, none reach the detector, so that region stays light.

options.text: The X-rays reflect off the bone and back to the camera.
options.rationale: 'Taking an X-ray' sounds like photography, which works by reflected light.

options.text: Bone is white in colour, so it appears white in the image.
options.rationale: A direct transfer of everyday colour to an image that is really a shadow.

mcqs.stem: Gamma rays are used both for medical imaging and for treatment. Which use is described correctly?

options.text: Gamma rays are never aimed at a patient, as they only cause harm.
options.rationale: Teaching about hazards leaves the single rule that ionising means harmful.

options.text: Gamma rays are shone in and reflect off a tumour to image it.
options.rationale: Imaging is assumed to work like photography, by reflection.

options.text: A beam of gamma rays is aimed at a tumour to destroy cancer cells.
options.rationale: This is the treatment application: the ionising effect of the beam kills the cells.

options.text: Gamma rays make a tumour glow so that a surgeon can see it.
options.rationale: Invents a visible effect; the gamma rays from a tracer are detected, not seen.

mcqs.stem: A house sits in a valley with a hill between it and the transmitter, yet the radio still receives a clear signal. Why?

options.text: Radio waves have long wavelengths, so they spread around the hill.
options.rationale: Spreading around an obstacle of this size is a property of the longest wavelengths, which is why radio waves suit broadcasting.

options.text: Radio waves travel faster than the other waves, so they get past it.
options.rationale: Speed is treated as the property that makes a wave good, though all travel at the same speed.

options.text: Radio waves are the most penetrating of all, so they pass through it.
options.rationale: Penetration and spreading around obstacles are merged into one idea of strength.

options.text: Radio waves are absorbed by the hill and then re-emitted behind it.
options.rationale: Absorption is real for some materials, but an absorbed wave does not reappear.

mcqs.stem: Why are microwaves, rather than long-wavelength radio waves, used to communicate with satellites?

options.text: Microwaves are reflected upwards by the atmosphere onto the satellite.
options.rationale: Reflection by the ionosphere is generalised into the way all signals travel.

options.text: Microwaves travel faster than radio waves, so they reach orbit sooner.
options.rationale: Speed is again taken to be the deciding property of a wave.

options.text: Microwaves are the only waves able to travel through empty space.
options.rationale: All electromagnetic waves cross a vacuum, so this cannot be the reason.

options.text: Microwaves pass through the atmosphere, while long radio waves are reflected.
options.rationale: Transmission through the atmosphere and the ionosphere is what allows the signal to reach orbit and return.

mcqs.stem: Why can a microwave oven heat a thick piece of food faster than a grill can?

options.text: Microwaves are absorbed at the centre, so the middle heats first.
options.rationale: The phrase 'cooks from the inside out' is taken literally.

options.text: Microwaves are infrared, which hot food absorbs very strongly.
options.rationale: The two neighbouring groups are treated as one kind of wave.

options.text: Microwaves make the warm food give out microwaves of its own.
options.rationale: Objects do emit infrared as they warm, but they do not re-emit microwaves.

options.text: Microwaves are absorbed by water a few centimetres into the food.
options.rationale: Energy is delivered throughout that outer layer rather than only to the surface, and conduction spreads it further.

mcqs.stem: Why does an electric bar heater warm a person standing in front of it in a cold room?

options.text: Infrared heats up the air first, and the warm air then heats the person.
options.rationale: Convection is the mechanism students meet most often for warming a room.

options.text: Infrared travels straight to the person and is absorbed by their skin.
options.rationale: Infrared is absorbed at the surface of whatever is in its path, transferring energy to it directly.

options.text: The heater emits microwaves, which are absorbed inside the body.
options.rationale: The two heating parts of the spectrum are treated as interchangeable.

options.text: The bar glows red, and it is that visible light which warms them.
options.rationale: The glow is what can be seen, so it is assumed to carry the energy.

mcqs.stem: A fibre optic cable bends round corners inside a building, yet the signal arrives undamaged. Which statement explains this?

options.text: The light reflects from the walls of the fibre, so it stays inside.
options.rationale: Reflection at the fibre wall keeps the light in the fibre as it follows the bend, and pure glass absorbs it weakly.

options.text: The cable has straight sections joined by tiny mirrors at each bend.
options.rationale: Invented by a student certain that light can only travel in straight lines.

options.text: The signal is really a microwave signal, which bends round corners.
options.rationale: Fibre broadband is merged with wireless signals travelling through the air.

options.text: The glass is dense enough to drag the light around every corner.
options.rationale: Density is misread as something that pulls a beam off a straight path.

mcqs.stem: Why does producing ultraviolet inside a fluorescent lamp make the lamp energy efficient?

options.text: The ultraviolet leaves the lamp and lights the room without heating.
options.rationale: The pairing of ultraviolet with the lamp suggests the ultraviolet is the output.

options.text: Ultraviolet is brighter than light, so less of it is needed to see.
options.rationale: Treats invisible ultraviolet as a very bright kind of visible light.

options.text: Ultraviolet carries no energy, so nothing at all is wasted in it.
options.rationale: Higher frequency means more energy, not less, so this cannot be the reason.

options.text: A coating turns the ultraviolet into visible light, so little is wasted.
options.rationale: Almost all the energy supplied is transferred by visible light rather than by heating a filament.

mcqs.stem: Why are gamma rays, rather than visible light, used to detect a tracer inside a patient's body?

options.text: Gamma rays reflect off the tracer and form a picture on a film.
options.rationale: Imaging is assumed to work by reflection, as photography does.

options.text: Gamma rays are harmless, so any dose at all may be used safely.
options.rationale: The dose is kept low precisely because gamma rays are ionising.

options.text: Gamma rays are penetrating, so they pass out of the body to a detector.
options.rationale: Only radiation that gets out through the tissue can be detected from outside the patient.

options.text: Visible light from the tracer would be much too dim to see through the skin.
options.rationale: Treats it as a brightness problem rather than one of absorption.

mcqs.stem: Why can X-rays and gamma rays be used to treat a tumour deep inside the body?

options.text: They are safe at any dose at all, so a large beam can be aimed anywhere.
options.rationale: The hazard is remembered as a rule about imaging only, not about dose.

options.text: They have longer wavelengths, which carry energy deep into the tissue.
options.rationale: Wavelength and penetrating power are merged into one idea of strength.

options.text: They penetrate the tissue and their ionising effect kills the cells.
options.rationale: Penetration gets the radiation to the tumour, and ionisation is what destroys the cancer cells.

options.text: They heat the tumour, like a grill would, until the cancer cells burn.
options.rationale: Transfers the heating effect of infrared to the far end of the spectrum.
